newsitem.title: RWANDA: Tide of refugees forces rethink on Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: Tide of refugees forces rethink on Zaire force.

text.p: After three days at full flood, the flow of refugees out of Zaire into Rwanda slowed on Monday and the world community struggled for consensus on whether a planned force to help the refugees was still needed.

The UNHCR estimated that 500,000 Hutu refugees were already back home in Rwanda and, with more still on the way, several countries -- barely able to hide their relief -- called for a radical rethink of the U.N.-approved force's size and aims.
Perhaps reflecting the lack of urgency now felt by those countries, a review meeting planned by the participants for Wednesday in Stuttgart, Germany, was put back to Thursday.

"I have been told that the meeting will be on Thursday," U.S. Navy Captain Timothy Taylor, director of public affairs for the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart, told Reuters. The European command will host the meeting to be led by Canada.
He had no explanation for the delay.

Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said Canada was determined to press ahead with the international rescue mission. "The mandate is still the same. We have to go there and we have to go for humanitarian purposes," he told a news conference in Ottawa.
However, Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young said a planned military force could be scaled back to simple humanitarian relief units if conditions continued to improve.

The Rwandan government, deeply suspicious of the intentions of the international community, went out of its way to speed the Hutus homewards, relaxing security at border posts and dropping plans to register the returnees.
It also took the first step in clearing refugee camps away from its border with Zaire on Monday.

Andrew Hall, a spokesman for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, said officials saying they were from the Rwandan Ministry of Rehabilitation closed down a Red Cross camp for 350 sick and exhausted refugees.
They ordered the Red Cross section inside Unbano camp to be closed and the 350 refugees were taken away in trucks.

"They didn't give specific reasons, or (said) only that they wanted the camps around the borders of Rwanda removed," he said. "There was no physical violence. Sticks were waved around, but they weren't used."
Unbano camp is the first unofficial camp reached by refugees trekking in from Zaire through the Rwandan town of Gisenyi. It is about four kms (two miles) from the border.
Zaire's Tutsi rebels, who have close links with Kigali, announced they would open a corridor in the Bukavu region so tens of thousands of refugees further south could also go home.

UNHCR spokesman Fernando Del Mundo said in Geneva the rebels told U.N. agencies that the corridor from Bukavu, south of Lake Kivu, to Rwanda's southwestern Cyangugu border crossing could be opened on Tuesday.
If those refugees start moving home, the argument in favour of the intervention force will be significantly weakened.
On Monday, Eritrea joined the chorus of countries saying the force was at best no longer necessary, at worst ill-conceived and said it was withdrawing an earlier commitment to take part.
In a statement faxed to Reuters in Nairobi, the foreign ministry said the wishes of regional leaders had been ignored.
Over a million Hutus fled Rwanda in mid-1994 after a rebel Tutsi army overran the country following the genocide of Tutsis by Hutu extremists. Many ended up in camps in eastern Zaire.

Fearing reprisals if they returned home, and terrified of the armed Hutu militants in their midst, the refugees stayed in their camps until an onslaught last month by Zairean rebels, including many Tutsis, forced the extremists to flee.

The United Nations appealed urgently to donors to provide $260 million to fund relief for the hundreds of thousands of refugees. The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA) said it would respond to the most urgent needs of of refugees, returnees and war displaced.
